content.title: Millions Of Americans Stripped Of Second Passport Rights Under New Citizenship Rule Change In Italy
content.text: via ShutterstockFor 160 years, Italy has offered citizenship by descent, which meant that any child of an Italian citizen is also an Italian citizen by default. However, in March 2025, the Italian government issued an emergency decree stripping many Italian descendants of that right.Though four judges fought back against the new legislation, it’s poised to pass. This means many Americans in the United States who are also hopeful Italian citizens and second passport holders may need to change their plans.This comes in the wake of other citizenship complications, like U.S. Senator Moreno's recent proposal that would force Americans to renounce dual citizenship and strip them of their second passports.How Italy's Citizenship Rules Are Changing And What It Means For Americans With Italian AncestryAny Americans who've been hoping for a future in Italy or even just the chance to hold Italian citizenship and passports based on their ancestors’ rights are set to lose out under recent law changes imposed by the Italian government.In the past, Italians who retained their own citizenship could pass it on to their children. A citizenship law passed in 1912 confirmed that Italians born and living abroad would retain their citizenship, regardless of their presence in Italy.The law was confirmed again in 1992. This effectively granted Italian citizenship to anyone with an ancestor alive after March 17, 1861, when the Kingdom of Italy was first established.However, last year’s emergency decree restricted Italian citizenship rights to individuals with a parent or grandparent who was born in Italy and who held solely Italian citizenship at the time of the descendant’s birth or the time of their own death, depending on which came first."Being an Italian citizen is a serious matter, the granting of citizenship is a serious matter," said Italy’s foreign minister Antonio Tajani. "Unfortunately over the years there have been abuses and requests for citizenship that went a bit beyond the true interest in our country."With this justification in mind, Tajani passed the emergency decree to change matters. This put a stop to the plans of many, including Americans, who were planning to claim citizenship and an Italian passport on the basis of a great-grandparent’s citizenship in the country.According to 2023 data, around 358,502 Italian citizens (those registered with the Registry of Italians Residing Abroad, or AIRE) live in the U.S.. But there are no officially logged numbers for Americans who would've been eligible for Italian citizenship based on their ancestry. Over 17 million Americans self-claim Italian ancestry, per U.S. census figures.With millions of Americans with Italian family and roots, the ruling means many of those Americans will no longer qualify for Italian citizenship and an Italian passport.Italy’s Constitutional Court Upheld The Emergency Decree, Banning Citizenship By DescentRobert Lyle Bolton, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia CommonsThough many fought back against the Italian government's emergency decree, the most recent court rulings indicate that the new citizenship rules are here to stay."The Constitutional Court has declared the questions of constitutional legitimacy raised by the Turin court partially unfounded and partially inadmissible," the court announced.An important distinction of the new law is that it doesn’t revoke descendants’ citizenship; it denies the existence of that citizenship. Still, this means that Americans who would've qualified for Italian citizenship by descent through their ancestors will be denied that right. There are only a few exceptions to the rule.Exceptions To Italy's New Citizenship RulesAs previously mentioned, Americans may still qualify for Italian citizenship if they have a parent or grandparent who currently holds exclusively Italian citizenship, or who held that citizenship at the time of death. However, this means that individuals with dual citizenship have given up the opportunity to pass their Italian citizenship on.Americans may also qualify for Italian citizenship if they have a parent or adoptive parent who resided in Italy for at least two consecutive years with Italian citizenship before their birth or adoption.Even if an American qualifies under one of these rules, they must still demonstrate proficiency in the Italian language to claim citizenship rights.Italian Citizens Celebrated The Ruling: No More Simplified Travel For Dual Nationals With Italian Passportsvia ShutterstockTajani’s ruling was targeted primarily at those who wanted dual national Italian citizenship as either a novelty or a means for easier travel. Many people have expressed support for the new rule, with comments like "Finally. Well done Italy.""Most countries that do citizenship by descent stop processing claims after grandparents. You have to strike a balance between being accommodating to your diaspora and acknowledging that heritage while still protecting the integrity of your citizenship," said one person commenting on 10 News’s coverage of the story.Another commenter got to the heart of the issue, which is the pursuit of citizenship for an easy Italian passport."There was a flood of applicants who wanted an Italian passport for reasons of optionality and not because they planned to relocate in Italy," they wrote on Instagram.Meanwhile, Americans who were in the process of pursuing Italian citizenship through their great-grandparents expressed devastation at the news. Some had been excited about the potential for their children to hold Italian passports, which is the type of situation Tajani wants to avoid.For travelers who had their sights set on an Italian passport to facilitate their travels abroad, the future doesn’t look bright. But travelers can still enter and enjoy Italy on other passports, even if they offer less novelty. They'll simply have to stick with their current citizenship and passport status if they're planning on visiting Italy.
